question: Under the Utah Timeshare and Camp Resort Act, how does a statutory "timeshare estate" differ from a "timeshare interest"?
choice_a: A timeshare estate always lasts less than one year, while a timeshare interest must last at least ten years
choice_b: A timeshare estate conveys a small, undivided fractional fee interest in the real property itself, while a timeshare interest is a right to occupy accommodations during three or more time periods over at least three years that need not include any estate in land
choice_c: A timeshare estate is exempt from state regulation, while a timeshare interest must be registered with the Division of Real Estate
choice_d: The two terms are legally interchangeable and Utah law draws no distinction between them
explanation: Utah Code 57-19-2 separately defines a "timeshare estate" as a small, undivided fractional fee interest in real property (i.e., an actual ownership interest in the land) and a "timeshare interest" as a contractual right to occupy fixed or variable accommodations during three or more separate time periods over a period of at least three years, whether or not coupled with an estate in land. This distinction is the real-world source of the exam outline's separate reference to "undivided fractionalized long-term estates."

question: Under the Utah Timeshare and Camp Resort Act (Utah Code Title 57, Chapter 19), who has authority to summarily deny a developer's or salesperson's registration application, subject to the applicant's right to request a hearing?
choice_a: The county recorder where the development is located
choice_b: The Utah Attorney General acting alone
choice_c: The director (of the Division of Real Estate)
choice_d: The homeowners' association board of the development
explanation: Utah Code 57-19-17 gives the director authority to summarily deny an application for registration under the Act, but the affected applicant may request a hearing, with further procedures for appeal to district court. Section 57-19-3 likewise gives the director authority to make, amend, and repeal rules necessary to carry out the Act.

question: Utah water law follows the prior appropriation doctrine rather than the riparian doctrine used in many eastern states. Under Utah Code 73-3-1, when two parties hold competing appropriative claims to the same water source, which claim has priority?
choice_a: The claim of whichever party owns land bordering the water source
choice_b: The claim of whichever party uses the largest total volume of water
choice_c: Priority is decided solely by the state engineer's discretion each year regardless of filing date
choice_d: The appropriator who is first in time is first in right
explanation: Utah Code 73-3-1 provides that a person may acquire a right to use unappropriated public water only for a useful and beneficial purpose, and that "between appropriators, the one first in time is first in rights" — the core "first in time, first in right" rule of the prior appropriation doctrine. The statute also specifies that water rights cannot be acquired by adverse use or adverse possession, in contrast to the riparian doctrine's focus on land ownership adjoining the water.

question: Under Utah Code 73-1-3, what serves as "the basis, the measure and the limit of all rights to the use of water" in the state?
choice_c: The date the deed to the adjoining land was recorded
choice_d: The volume specified in the original homestead patent
explanation: Utah Code 73-1-3 states in full: "Beneficial use shall be the basis, the measure and the limit of all rights to the use of water in this state." A water right holder who fails to put the water to beneficial use risks forfeiture, and the extent of beneficial use caps the size of the right.

question: To preserve the ability to later claim a construction (mechanic's) lien in Utah, a contractor, subcontractor, or material supplier generally must file a preliminary notice with the state construction registry no later than how many days after commencing construction work on the project?
explanation: Utah Code 38-1a-501 requires a person who desires to claim a construction lien to file a preliminary notice with the state construction registry no later than 20 days after the day the person commences providing construction work. A person who fails to file a timely preliminary notice may not claim a construction lien; late filing is possible in limited circumstances but forfeits lien rights for work performed before the notice, and a preliminary notice has no effect if filed more than 10 days after a notice of completion is filed.

question: Absent a recorded notice of completion, a Utah construction lien claimant must record a claim of lien within how many days after final completion of the original contract in order to preserve the lien?
explanation: Utah Code 38-1a-502 sets the deadline to record a claim of lien at 180 days after final completion of the original contract, or, if a notice of completion is filed, 90 days after that filing (but never more than 180 days after final completion). The claimant must also deliver or mail a copy of the recorded lien to the owner within 30 days of filing.

question: Under Utah's Residence Lien Restriction and Lien Recovery Fund Act (Utah Code Title 38, Chapter 11), a residential owner is protected from a subcontractor's or supplier's lien for nonpayment further down the contracting chain when the owner has:
choice_a: Paid every subcontractor and supplier directly, bypassing the general contractor entirely
choice_b: Recorded a homestead exemption on the property before construction began
choice_c: Purchased an owner's title insurance policy naming the contractor as an additional insured
choice_d: Entered a written contract with an original contractor (licensed or exempt from licensure) or qualifying developer/retailer, and paid that party in full in accordance with the contract and any amendments
explanation: Utah Code 38-11-204 protects an owner from a residential lien where the owner (or the owner's agent) entered a written contract with a licensed or license-exempt original contractor, real estate developer, or factory-built housing retailer, and paid that party in full under the contract, and that party then failed to pay a qualified beneficiary (an unpaid downstream subcontractor or supplier).

question: Under Utah Code 38-11-204, an unpaid subcontractor or supplier (a "qualified beneficiary") seeking payment from the Residence Lien Recovery Fund must obtain a judgment against the nonpaying contractor by filing suit within how many days of filing a notice of claim (or, if earlier, within 270 days of contract completion)?
explanation: Utah Code 38-11-204 requires the qualified beneficiary to file an action against the nonpaying original contractor, developer, or retailer and obtain a judgment within 180 days of filing a notice of claim, or 270 days after completion of the contract, whichever is earlier, and to pursue supplemental collection proceedings before recovering from the fund.

question: In Utah, unpaid general property taxes become a lien against the real property as of what date each year?
explanation: Utah Code 59-2-1302 provides that property taxes attach as a lien upon the owner's real property as of noon on January 1 of each year.

question: Under Utah Code 59-2-1343, real property becomes subject to the county's final tax sale process once property taxes have been delinquent for how many years without redemption by the following March 15?
explanation: Utah Code 59-2-1343 provides that if delinquent property taxes are not redeemed by March 15 following the lapse of four years from the date of delinquency, the property becomes subject to the county's tax sale process (with a limited exception for properties under an approved tax deferral).

question: In a Utah trust deed (deed of trust) financing arrangement, which three parties are involved, and what is the trustee's role?
choice_a: The buyer, the seller, and the county recorder, with the recorder holding title until the loan is paid
choice_b: The mortgagor, the mortgagee, and a notary public who witnesses the closing
choice_c: The grantor, the grantee, and the title insurance company, which holds legal title during the loan term
choice_d: The trustor (borrower/property owner), the beneficiary (lender), and the trustee — a person to whom title is conveyed in trust to secure performance of the obligation and who may exercise the power of sale on default
explanation: Utah Code 57-1-19 defines the trust deed structure: the trustor conveys real property by trust deed to a trustee, who holds title in trust to secure performance of an obligation owed to the beneficiary. Because the trustee holds title, a qualified trustee can exercise a power of sale to conduct a nonjudicial foreclosure if the trustor defaults, without going through the courts.

question: Utah is a deed-of-trust (nonjudicial foreclosure) state. Under Utah Code 57-1-24, once a qualified trustee records a notice of default on a trust deed, how much time must elapse before the trustee may proceed with the trustee's sale?
explanation: Utah Code 57-1-24 allows a qualified trustee to exercise the power of sale, without judicial proceedings, only after recording a notice of default and then waiting until not less than three months have elapsed from the time the notice of default was filed for record, after which notice of sale must be given under sections 57-1-25 and 57-1-26.

question: At a Utah trustee's sale conducted under a power of sale in a trust deed (Utah Code 57-1-27), who is permitted to bid on the property at the public auction?
choice_a: Only pre-qualified third-party investors registered with the county
choice_b: Any person, including the beneficiary or the trustee, may bid at the sale
choice_d: Only licensed Utah real estate brokers acting on behalf of a client
explanation: Utah Code 57-1-27 requires the trustee (or the trustee's attorney) to sell the trust property at public auction to the highest bidder, and expressly allows any person, including the beneficiary or trustee, to bid at the sale.

question: Utah maintains a public, internet-accessible Sex, Kidnap, and Child Abuse Offender Registry under Utah Code Title 77, Chapter 41. Before a member of the public may view offender information on the registry website, the site requires the user to acknowledge a disclaimer stating that:
choice_a: The information may be resold to any commercial tenant-screening or background-check business without restriction
choice_b: Real estate licensees are legally required to disclose registry search results to every buyer before closing
choice_c: Members of the public are not allowed to use the information to harass or threaten offenders or members of their families
choice_d: Offenders listed on the registry may bring a civil suit against the state for maintaining their listing
explanation: Utah Code 77-41-110 requires the department to maintain a public, internet-accessible registry, but requires users to acknowledge a disclaimer that the information may not be used to harass or threaten offenders or their families. The statute also grants the department and its personnel immunity from civil liability for good-faith compliance with the registry chapter.

question: A house was the site of a highly publicized death several years ago, but the event had no effect on the home's physical condition. Under Utah Code 57-1-37, what are the seller's and listing agent's obligations regarding disclosure of this "stigmatized" fact to a prospective buyer?
choice_a: Disclosure is mandatory any time the buyer is a first-time homebuyer
choice_b: The fact must be included in the seller's written property condition disclosure regardless of physical impact
choice_c: Disclosure is required only if the buyer's lender specifically asks about it in writing
choice_d: Neither the owner nor the owner's agent is required to disclose that the property is stigmatized, and neither is liable for failing to disclose it
explanation: Utah Code 57-1-37 provides that the failure of an owner to disclose that property being offered for sale is stigmatized is not a material fact that must be disclosed, and that neither the owner nor the owner's agent is liable for failing to disclose that a property is stigmatized.
